rationale: A wins because it keeps the sharpest story inside the facts: "The retailer that won't say how much money its sustainability story makes" turns Patagonia's nondisclosure into a real scrutiny angle without inventing the economics. B has better desk targeting, but "Patagonia puts a repair counter in every US store" and "has nothing new to sell" smuggle in premises the update does not prove. That's useful raw material, but it needs an editor before a founder uses it.
gaps_in_A: "sustainable-fashion or circular-economy trade reporter" is serviceable but still a little broad; B gets closer to actual desks like retail operations and consumer service.
"the repair and resale programs are being expanded as described" overstates the update. Repair is expanding; resale only has a 500,000-item cumulative disclosure here.
"Next step: `newsjack-detector`" may overcomplicate a same-day company launch. If pitching the repair rollout, journalist fit and proof gathering matter more than hunting for an outside peg.
gaps_in_B: "Patagonia puts a repair counter in every US store" invents a physical or operational detail. The update says customers can drop items off at stores, not that each store has a repair counter or performs repairs on site.

"Patagonia's newest store rollout has nothing new to sell" overreads "no new apparel line announced." Patagonia still sells apparel; absence from this announcement is not proof of a no-new-product strategy.
"what it costs to staff 70-plus locations for it" assumes store-level repair staffing before proving whether repairs happen in store or through a central facility.

"private owner that directs profits to environmental causes" is sloppy sourcing. The update says Patagonia is privately held and directs profits to environmental causes; it does not prove ownership structure caused this rollout.
